transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-10
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Morales (Redwood AE), Daniel Kim (Redwood SE), Mark Reynolds (Crestview Head of Security), Aisha Patel (VP of Cloud), Tom Nguyen (Compliance Officer)

[00:00] Sofia Morales: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, really appreciate it. I'm Sofia, I'm the AE on the account, and with me is Daniel from the engineering team. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Mark Reynolds: Good, thanks. We've got about 45 minutes, right? Focused on data residency and compliance questions.
[00:12] Sofia Morales: Yep, that's the plan. We put together a short agenda — quick intros, your constraints and regulatory requirements, then we'll walk options (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private), logging/audit behavior, encryption and KMS, and then next steps.
[00:22] Aisha Patel: Sounds good. Quick context: Crestview runs core banking in AWS us-east-2, we have strict data residency for EU customers, and for some product lanes we need to ensure no export of PII outside the approved regions.
[00:32] Tom Nguyen: And from compliance, we're tracking both EU GDPR and US financial regs; for certain datasets HIPAA-like controls are required even though it's not healthcare, basically we need encryption at rest in our control and complete audit trails.
[00:42] Daniel Kim: Thanks for that. Quick question: when you say "no export of PII", is that for storage of logs, model inputs/outputs, or both?
[00:49] Mark Reynolds: Ideally both. We can't have customer-identifiable prompts or transcripts stored in a central US location if the customer is EU-resident. We also want the ability to redact or not persist logs at all for certain routes.
[00:58] Sofia Morales: Understood. High level: Redwood Hosted keeps data in regionally isolated clusters and we offer region selection for hosted API; however, Hosted still has Redwood-managed keys by default and logs stored to our analytics buckets. For stricter requirements we usually recommend Redwood Dedicated (reserved capacity in a customer-dedicated pool) or Redwood Private (VPC or on-prem) so keys and logs can be customer-managed and isolated.
[01:23] Mark Reynolds: Can you clarify the difference between Dedicated and Private from a key-control and logging perspective?
[01:28] Daniel Kim: Sure — Dedicated is reserved GPU pools that are logically isolated for a customer in our infra. We can offer bring-your-own-key via KMS integrations so you control master keys if you want. Audit logs and telemetry are still streamed to the customer VPC or customer-managed S3 if required. Private goes a step further — the control plane can be run in your VPC or on-prem; we can ship an air-gapped appliance in extreme cases. In Private, you manage keys entirely (HSM/KMS), and Redwood does not retain request payloads unless you opt in.
[01:53] Aisha Patel: So for Dedicated, the compute is still in Redwood datacenter or cloud accounts, but we can host logs in our S3?
[01:59] Daniel Kim: Exactly. Compute runs in our managed fleet but we can set up a VPC peering or private link and push logs to your account. Data residency is preserved for persisted artifacts. For ephemeral tokens in cache, those are managed in-memory and not written to logs by default.
[02:14] Tom Nguyen: About model caching and KV cache — if someone uploads user prompts, we need to ensure KV cache doesn't persist across regions or get checkpointed. Is that something you can guarantee?
[02:22] Daniel Kim: KV cache is in-memory, per-instance, and isn't persisted to long-term storage unless we snapshot for debugging. For customers with strict rules we can disable snapshotting and ensure debug dumps are filtered. That's part of our Dedicated/Private playbook.
[02:36] Mark Reynolds: GDPR specifically — we need the ability to delete user data on request and have proof of deletion. How does Redwood support right-to-be-forgotten requests?
[02:44] Sofia Morales: For Hosted we provide APIs to purge customer data from our retention stores; for Dedicated/Private, since logs and artifacts can be routed to your storage, deletion is typically in your control. We also keep audit trails of deletion actions. We'll send the documented flow in the security pack.
[02:58] Aisha Patel: Encryption at rest — we want customer keys in our KMS (we use AWS KMS) and HSM-backed keys for the most sensitive lanes. Can you integrate with our KMS?
[03:06] Daniel Kim: Yes, we support AWS KMS customer-managed keys for Dedicated. For Private, you have full control, and we can also integrate with on-prem HSMs where network allows. For Hosted, BYOK is more limited; we can discuss exceptions but default Hosted uses Redwood-managed keys.
[03:19] Mark Reynolds: Okay. Logging and PII — we need an option to redact or not log prompts for certain endpoints. Is that configurable on a per-route basis?
[03:26] Daniel Kim: Yes. We provide per-route logging and retention policies. You can configure routes that never persist prompts or mask tokens at ingestion time. We also have quality-monitoring hooks that can run on sampled traffic only if you opt in.
[03:39] Tom Nguyen: What about SOC 2 and HIPAA attestation? We need to see audits and policies.
[03:44] Sofia Morales: We have SOC 2 Type II, and we maintain a HIPAA compliance pack covering our BAAs and controls when a BAA is signed. I'll attach those documents.
[03:52] Mark Reynolds: Can you confirm that Redwood will sign a BAA and also support contractual language for data residency?
[03:57] Sofia Morales: Yes, we do sign BAAs for customers where the use case requires it. For data residency, we can include contractual commitments for region controls as part of the enterprise contract for Dedicated or Private.
[04:08] Aisha Patel: Latency concern — if we keep data strictly in eu-west-1 for EU customers, does performance degrade vs. central US? We run high throughput customer-facing assistants.
[04:16] Daniel Kim: There is a small performance delta depending on region and instance types. Our Dedicated fleet can provision GPUs in eu-west-1, and we can size throughput accordingly. We also have compilers and optimizations tuned per-region. We'll propose an SLA and a benchmark plan.
[04:29] Mark Reynolds: On the topic of model variants and fallback — we sometimes want a fallback to a smaller local model if the primary hosted model is overloaded. How do you handle model variant routing with residency constraints?
[04:38] Daniel Kim: Smart routing supports policy-based routing. You can set policies by region, latency, and cost. If a fallback is needed, it must be to a model instance that satisfies residency rules; we can configure regional model caches or dedicated local variants to ensure policy compliance.
[04:54] Tom Nguyen: About audit logs, what level of detail is captured? We need user IDs, timestamps, route called, and retention for seven years for some regs.
[05:02] Sofia Morales: We capture event-level logs with request metadata and timestamp. We can push logs to your logging pipeline (Splunk/Datadog/S3) for long-term retention. We can also redact sensitive fields before export if required.
[05:11] Mark Reynolds: Is there an option to keep only non-identifiable telemetry in Redwood's analytics while all identifiable logs go to our account?
[05:17] Daniel Kim: Yes — differential telemetry is supported. We can configure ingestion to split telemetry: anonymized usage metrics to Redwood analytics and detailed PII-containing logs to your sinks.
[05:27] Aisha Patel: Any blockers around legal/regulatory export controls? For example, if we have customers in the EU, we cannot transfer certain financial analysis outside of region.
[05:35] Sofia Morales: We work with customers to map data flows. For strict non-export cases, Private deployment or on-prem is recommended. We also have contractual assurances and technical controls for Dedicated. We'll include a data-flow diagram in the follow-up.
[05:47] Mark Reynolds: Are there limitations for on-prem? E.g., features that only Hosted offers like certain analytics dashboards?
[05:53] Daniel Kim: The Console features are available for Private as long as network connectivity to the control plane is configured. For fully air-gapped on-prem, some SaaS console features are replaced by local monitoring stacks; we provide equivalent APIs and Grafana dashboards. We'll clarify feature parity in the pack.
[06:08] Tom Nguyen: Can you walk through a sample data lifecycle for an EU user prompt to a customer-facing assistant? I'd like to hear timestamps: ingestion, caching, model forward, logs written, retention.
[06:16] Daniel Kim: Sure — sample flow for Dedicated in eu-west-1: 1) Ingestion at the regional edge (t=0), 2) Tokenization and in-memory KV cache (t=+10ms), 3) Model forward on regional GPU (t=+40ms), 4) Response returned to client (t=+50ms), 5) If route is configured to persist, a masked copy of request and response is pushed to your S3 in eu-west-1 (t=+200ms). No payloads leave the region. If the route is configured as non-persisted, step 5 is skipped.
[06:44] Aisha Patel: That flow helps. For GDPR erasure, the S3 copies are in our account so we can delete them; but what about ephemeral traces in Redwood logs or monitoring?
[06:52] Daniel Kim: Ephemeral monitoring traces are kept with a configurable TTL and can be set to not contain PII. For Hosted, we have purge APIs. For Dedicated/Private, we default to routing to your storage so deletion is under your control.
[07:06] Mark Reynolds: What about change management and access controls? We need RBAC, SSO, and audit of admin actions.
[07:12] Sofia Morales: We support SSO/SAML for user access, RBAC for roles, and all admin operations are logged. For Dedicated and Private we can integrate with your SCIM/IdP and map roles accordingly.
[07:22] Tom Nguyen: If we choose Dedicated, how long does procurement/standup take? We need to plan a pilot by end of Q1.
[07:27] Sofia Morales: Typical timeline for Dedicated: contract and procurement ~3-4 weeks, infra provisioning ~2 weeks, pilot run and benchmarks ~2 weeks — so roughly 7-8 weeks from signed contract to pilot, depending on procurement speed. Private on-prem is longer due to install and networking, usually 8-12 weeks.
[07:42] Mark Reynolds: Are there standard pricing or additional costs for encryption-by-customer-key and log routing?
[07:47] Sofia Morales: There are add-on fees for private-control-plane or dedicated regional capacity, and some integrations (HSM connectors, extended retention) have line items. We'll include a draft commercial sheet in the follow-up.
[07:58] Aisha Patel: For the benchmarking, we'll want a small POC with 10k requests/day and some larger variance tests. Can you run that in eu-west-1 and show latency percentiles?
[08:06] Daniel Kim: Yes. We'll propose a benchmark with p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, and cost per token. We'll also include a stress test to validate autoscaling.
[08:15] Mark Reynolds: One last question on data lineage: we need to show auditors a chain of custody for certain data flows. Can Redwood provide exportable lineage logs?
[08:22] Daniel Kim: We can provide exportable audit logs that show request IDs, timestamps, and storage location. Combined with your S3 lifecycle events you should be able to form a chain of custody report.
[08:34] Sofia Morales: Great. Quick recap of next steps: we'll send SOC2/HIPAA docs and the security pack, Daniel will put together a dedicated architecture + benchmark plan, and Mark will share Crestview's regulatory doc and allowed regions. Does that capture it?
[08:46] Mark Reynolds: Yep. Also please include a sample BAA and example contract language for region guarantees.
[08:52] Sofia Morales: Will do. Anything else from your side?
[08:55] Aisha Patel: No, that's it for now. Looking forward to the security pack.
[08:59] Tom Nguyen: Thanks all.
[09:01] Sofia Morales: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the docs and calendar invites for the technical deep-dive.
